paragraphs: Cumberland Council does not run fostering on its own: it is part of Cumbria Fostering, one hosted service shared with Westmorland and Furness Council, while each council still carries out the assessments of its own carers. Children in care here are looked after by that service and by independent agencies, including those shown above.

In May 2026 Cumberland Council said there were around 730 children in care in Cumbria and around 275 carers, and that the strongest need was for homes for brothers and sisters, older children and children with more complex needs. Its sufficiency strategy for 2024 to 2027 adds disabled children, teenagers, larger sibling groups and young people who arrived in the UK alone, as well as carers who can look after a parent together with their baby. The same strategy recorded 219 mainstream foster families, with eight households joining in a year and 18 leaving, mostly on retirement.

Cumberland used Department for Education funding to start its first Mockingbird group, in which an experienced hub carer and a liaison worker support six to ten fostering families who live near each other. The council also takes part in Foster With Us, a recruitment hub shared with Westmorland and Furness, Lancashire, Blackpool and Blackburn with Darwen councils, which answers first enquiries.

Cumbria Fostering runs information events through the year; during Foster Care Fortnight in May 2026 they included Workington Library and an online session, and no booking was needed for the drop-ins. Single people are welcome to apply, as are people who work.
Ask the council and two or three of the agencies above how far children travel to school and family time, and what training and support is close to you.
